claims.text: The baseline AlCoCrFeNi HEA is produced by conventional casting and homogenization.
The baseline alloy has a relatively heterogeneous and coarse-grained microstructure.
Cold rolling followed by annealing near 800°C and controlled cooling will refine the grain structure.
The treatment will produce an optimal nanograined microstructure.
The treatment will stabilize predominantly high-angle grain boundaries.
An optimally refined grain size increases yield strength through the Hall–Petch mechanism.
The engineered fine-grained structure impedes dislocation movement.
Impeded dislocation movement reduces room-temperature creep.
Stabilized high-angle grain boundaries reduce the continuity of corrosion-vulnerable microstructural features.
Reducing the continuity of vulnerable microstructural features limits corrosion pathways.
The treatment will improve mechanical durability relative to the untreated baseline.
The treated alloy will have greater yield strength than the untreated alloy.
The treated alloy will have a lower room-temperature creep rate than the untreated alloy.
The treated alloy will have better corrosion resistance than the untreated alloy.
The predicted improvements depend on maintaining grain size within an optimal window.
Excessive grain refinement may negate the benefits or produce inverse Hall–Petch behavior.
The improvements are expected under room-temperature loading.
The improvements are expected in typical aerospace corrosive environments.

contradictions.description: The boundary explicitly predicts that excessive refinement outside the optimized processing window may cause inverse Hall–Petch behavior, whereas the falsification rule treats observation of that behavior under excessive refinement as falsifying the hypothesis. An anticipated off-window failure does not logically falsify the conditional claim about an optimally processed sample.
